name: Wood type
summary: Large display letters cut from end-grain wood, so a printer can set a heavy headline that metal type cannot give at that size.
how: Set the headline at 5 to 30 cm cap height; below 2 cm use metal type.
Use heavy weights: a stem of 1/5 to 1/3 of the cap height.
Mix two to four faces in one sheet, one face for each line, with each line set to the full measure.
Keep the line spacing tight: 1.0 to 1.1 times the cap height.

origin.note: Darius Wells cuts display letters from end-grain wood with a router and sells them to printers.

adoptions.via: William Leavenworth adds the pantograph to the router; one pattern then gives each size, and slab and grotesque faces spread to every job printer.
Trade cards and shop signs set the name of the firm in heavy wood letters.
Rob Roy Kelly publishes American Wood Type 1828–1900, and designers take the faces back into posters.

sources.title: Rob Roy Kelly, American Wood Type 1828–1900 (1969)
